messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
At 48 years old, Miriam had dedicated her life to her calling as a rabbi, guiding her community through both joyful and painful moments. But an event in her past had cast a long shadow over her present. It had been two years since a devastating explosion rocked her town during a community event, the very gathering she had organized to foster connection and healing. The chaos that ensued had left a deep imprint on her psyche; the shattering sound of the blast echoed not only in her ears but also in her mind, replaying relentlessly whenever she encountered loud noises, even the pop of a firecracker during a summer gathering. The sound of an explosion could send her heart racing, causing her to feel as if she were right back in that moment of terror, surrounded by panic and confusion.

Miriam had come to believe that her community, her home, and even her own perception of safety had been irrevocably shattered. This belief that the world was a dangerous place only intensified her need to engage in avoidance strategies, as she thought it was the only way to protect herself from further harm. The constant sense of danger she felt reinforced this belief, leading her to conclude that she was no longer the person she once was; the world had become a place where she could not feel secure. This belief only deepened her conviction that she was weak and vulnerable, reinforcing a sense of helplessness that made her avoid situations where she might feel exposed or threatened. This belief took root in the weeks following the explosion, as she found herself struggling with feelings of inaction guilt. Each act of avoidance only reinforced her negative appraisals, convincing her that she was more fragile than others and incapable of coping with the world outside her self-imposed boundaries. In her mind, if she felt weak and vulnerable, it made sense to avoid situations that might expose her further, as staying away from triggers felt like the only rational choice she had. She was convinced that she could have done more, that somehow her presence could have shielded her congregation from the horror that unfolded. This guilt manifested in various ways; she began to avoid discussing the event with others, fearing that even a mention might upset them or draw her back into the depths of that traumatic experience. However, each time she resorted to silence and avoidance, she felt a quiet accumulation of evidence that perhaps she was more fragile than others, reinforcing her belief that she couldn't cope without these strategies. Each act of avoidance deepened her conviction that she was incapable of managing her emotions, making her feel more fragile and reinforcing the idea that she could not handle the world as it was now. She stopped engaging in conversations about safety and security, believing it was better to remain silent than to risk triggering anyone else's memories or her own. As her avoidance grew, it turned into an unintentional map of her trauma, marking the places she could no longer visit and the subjects she could no longer discuss, which only served to amplify her feelings of isolation and fear. These maladaptive strategies became direct reminders of her trauma, as each avoided location or topic solidified her belief that she was trapped in a life defined by fear and vulnerability. Each place she avoided became a reminder of her trauma, and the routes she no longer took transformed into silent acknowledgments of her past, creating a world that felt increasingly small and confining.

The threat of danger loomed large in Miriam's life, casting a pall over her daily activities. This constant sense of threat fed into her negative appraisals, leading her to feel that she was no longer the person she once was and that safety was an unattainable illusion. This constant sense of danger served as the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair, leading her to internalize the belief that she was no longer the person she once was. Nights were particularly challenging; darkness seemed to amplify her fears, making her acutely aware of every sound that broke the silence. She would lie awake, scanning the shadows of her bedroom and the outlines of her home, convinced that danger lurked just beyond her sight. It was during these sleepless nights that she felt the weight of her negative appraisals most heavily; she could not shake the feeling that nothing good would ever come to her again. Each moment of peace felt like a prelude to inevitable chaos, and this pervasive sense of unease tightened her shoulders and quickened her breath.

As Miriam's vigilance intensified, she began to withdraw from her husband. Their intimate moments became tinged with anxiety, the very thought of sexual intimacy triggering a sense of vulnerability that she could not bear. She couldn’t help but feel that exposing herself emotionally and physically would only invite more chaos into her life. This avoidance strategy reinforced her belief that safety was an illusion; she felt that no matter how much her husband reassured her, she could never truly trust that they were safe. Her growing need to protect herself through avoidance continually reminded her of her fragility, leading her to believe that if she needed these strategies to cope, it proved she was not getting better. This self-imposed isolation began to erode the foundation of their relationship, leaving her feeling more desolate and disconnected.

Yet, despite the turmoil within her, Miriam continued to fulfill her responsibilities as a rabbi. She led services and offered counsel to her community, but inside, she felt like a hollow shell. The very environment that had once brought her joy now felt fraught with danger, and she found herself scanning the room for signs of threat even while delivering a sermon. Each time she sensed a member of her congregation watching her, she felt a surge of panic, convinced that they could see through her façade. The weight of her negative appraisals seemed to be mirrored in their eyes, amplifying her insecurities and fears.

Miriam's struggles reached a breaking point when she realized she could no longer bear the burden of her pain alone. It was during a particularly unsettling night, consumed by thoughts of danger and guilt, that she finally reached out for help. The toll it had taken on her marriage and her ability to serve her community prompted her to seek guidance from a therapist. She was terrified of what lay ahead, fearing that confronting her trauma might unearth feelings she had spent so long suppressing. Yet, she also held a flicker of hope that perhaps, through this journey, she could reclaim her sense of safety, rebuild her connection to her husband, and rediscover the joy that had once filled her life.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not explicitly convey that negative appraisals lead to the use of maladaptive strategies; it describes both but lacks a clear causal connection.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not establish a direct connection showing that the sense of threat is what leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: While maladaptive strategies are mentioned, the vignette does not explicitly state that they reinforce negative appraisals, leaving that causal link unmade.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This belief that the world was a dangerous place only intensified her need to engage in avoidance strategies, as she thought it was the only way to protect herself from further harm.  
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>  
If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenseless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do.  
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This constant sense of danger served as the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair, leading her to internalize the belief that she was no longer the person she once was.  
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>  
Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe.  
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Each act of avoidance only reinforced her negative appraisals, convincing her that she was more fragile than others and incapable of coping with the world outside her self-imposed boundaries.  
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>  
Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now.  
<<<END>>>
